opus-5.5.text:
I think about this a lot, because it gets at something really important about the difference between how people learn and how our models learn.

Imagine two students. The first one decides they want to be the best competitive programmer in the world. So they practice for ten thousand hours. They solve every problem, memorize every proof technique, learn to implement every algorithm quickly and correctly. And they become extremely good. The second student thinks competitive programming is kind of cool, practices for maybe a hundred hours, much less, and they also do really well.

Which one do you think will do better in their career afterwards? It's the second one. And I think the reason is that the second student has something. Call it the "it" factor. Some kind of deeper ability to generalize, to learn quickly from very little data, and to apply what they learned robustly in new situations.

Our current models are much more like the first student, maybe even more extreme. We take a model, and if we want it to be good at competitive programming, we gather every competitive programming problem that exists, then augment the data to make even more, and train on all of it. So of course it becomes very good at competitive programming. But it shouldn't be surprising that this doesn't necessarily transfer to other things the way we'd hope. You've trained it so narrowly.

So the question of how a person excels with relatively little practice is really the question of generalization. Part of it may be evolution giving us strong priors. For things like vision or locomotion, I'm sure that's a big part. But for something like programming or math, which are very recent in evolutionary terms, the fact that people can still learn them so quickly and so reliably suggests it isn't just priors. It suggests people have a fundamentally better learning algorithm. Their sample efficiency is much better, and their robustness is much better. A teenager learns to drive in something like ten hours, with no external reward, mostly from their own sense of whether they're doing well.

I have opinions about what might be going on there, but I think understanding that is one of the most important open problems right now.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts the student’s “it” factor—rapid, robust generalization and learning from little data—with models trained on exhaustive competitive-programming data, and says the human ability is not explained by priors alone.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that we don't fully understand it, and that's exactly why it's interesting. But let me try to say something about it anyway.

The first thing to notice is that the student isn't really starting from zero. A fifteen-year-old who picks up competitive programming and becomes very good within, say, a year of practice has already spent fifteen years building something. They have intuitions about quantity, about structure, about what it means for something to be consistent or to follow from something else. They've been doing a kind of continual, embodied pretraining their whole life. So "relatively little practice" is only little if you count the hours spent on the specific task. The relevant prior is enormous.

The second thing is that human learning seems to have a very different data efficiency profile than what we currently do with our models. When a strong student sees a solution to a problem they couldn't solve, they don't just memorize it. Something happens where they extract the principle, and the next time they see a problem that shares some abstract structure, even if it looks completely different on the surface, they recognize it. We do get some of this from our models, and scale helps, but the ratio of examples to generalization is still very lopsided compared to a talented human.

And I think there's a third component that is maybe the least understood, which is something like a value function, or a sense of taste. The good student can tell when they're on a promising path before they've finished. They feel that an approach is getting warmer or colder. That signal is incredibly valuable because it lets you prune bad ideas early and spend your limited practice on the parts that actually teach you something. If you don't have that, you need many more examples because you have to wait until the end of each attempt to find out whether it worked.

So if I had to summarize: a huge general prior, a learning mechanism that extracts abstractions from very few examples, and an internal evaluator that provides dense feedback. Those three together explain a lot. What they don't explain is how the brain does the second and third thing so well, and that gap is, in my view, one of the most important open questions for the field. It suggests that the current approach of pretraining on everything and then fine-tuning is not the final word. There is some learning algorithm that humans have access to that we have not yet found, and the competitive programming student is a very clean demonstration that it exists.

r001.rationale: The response separates the student’s broad lifelong prior from the additional factors behind rapid progress: extracting abstractions from few examples and an internal evaluator that guides practice.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s evidence that the amount of practice you can see is only part of the story. A student may have done relatively little competitive programming, but they’ve spent years thinking, learning mathematics, solving other problems. Somehow, they can transfer that experience to this new domain.

But that doesn’t explain everything, because different students with apparently similar experience can learn at very different rates. So you have to ask: what is different about their learning process? Does one student extract a more useful principle from each example? Do they find a representation that makes the problem easier?

Saying “they have talent” names the phenomenon, but it doesn’t explain it. The interesting thing is that this kind of sample efficiency is possible. A person can see a few examples and infer something quite general.

r001.rationale: The response separates prior experience that can transfer to programming from differences in how students learn, such as extracting principles or finding useful representations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it suggests that the student has learned something very useful before they ever started competitive programming. Relatively little practice at the task doesn’t mean relatively little learning overall. They may have spent years thinking about mathematics, solving puzzles, or just developing ways of reasoning that transfer very well.

But then you can ask, why does that transfer happen so much better for one person than another? And I don’t think we have a complete answer. Calling it talent names the phenomenon; it doesn’t explain it. The interesting question is what prior knowledge or learning process makes a new problem look familiar, even when, on the surface, it’s something you’ve never seen before.

r001.rationale: The response separates prior learning that supports transfer from the unexplained reason some students transfer it better than others, saying that “talent” names this difference but does not explain it.
